senses.definition: (in the singular) The ability to see.
examples: He is losing his sight and now can barely read.

quotes.text: Thy sight is young, / And thou shalt read when mine begin to dazzle.

senses.definition: The act of seeing; perception of objects by the eye; view.

quotes.text: And when hee had spoken these things, while they beheld, hee was taken vp, and a cloud receiued him out of their sight.

senses.definition: (often in the plural) Something worth seeing; a spectacle, either good or bad.
examples: We went to London and saw all the sights – Buckingham Palace, Tower Bridge, and so on.
You really look a sight in that ridiculous costume!

quotes.text: And Moses saide, I will nowe turne aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.
quotes.reference: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London: […] Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 3:3:

quotes.text: They never saw a sight so fair.

senses.definition: (often in the plural) A device used in aiming a projectile, through which the person aiming looks at the intended target.
A small aperture through which objects are to be seen, and by which their direction is settled or ascertained.

quotes.text: their eyes of fire sparking through sights of steel
quotes.reference: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]. Epilogue.”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:

senses.definition: (now colloquial) a great deal, a lot; frequently used to intensify a comparative.
examples: This is a darn sight better than what I'm used to at home!

quotes.text:
"If your mother put you in the pit at twelve, it's no reason why I should do the same with my lad."
"Twelve! It wor a sight afore that!"

senses.definition: In a drawing, picture, etc., that part of the surface, as of paper or canvas, which is within the frame or the border or margin. In a frame, the open space, the opening.
(obsolete) The instrument of seeing; the eye.

quotes.text: Why cloude they not their ſights perpetually,

senses.definition: (transitive) To see; to get sight of (something); to register visually.
examples: to sight land from a ship

quotes.text: I was on my way to the door, but all at once, through the fog in my head, I began to sight one reef that I hadn't paid any attention to afore.
quotes.reference: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter IV, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y.; London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:

subsenses.definition: (transitive) To observe through, or as if through, a sight, to check the elevation, direction, levelness, or other characteristics of, especially when surveying or navigating.

quotes.text: Next a point of known elevation, preferably one of the triangulation stations, is sighted; the vertical angle is read and the horizontal distance is scaled from the point of the setup on the map to the point sighted.
quotes.reference: 1912, John Herbert Farrell, Alfred Joseph Moses, Practical Field Geology, page 30:

senses.definition: (transitive) To apply sights to; to adjust the sights of.
examples: to sight a rifle or a cannon

senses.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To observe or aim (at something) using a (gun) sight.

quotes.text: Jim braced the gun and sighted, tried to pull the trigger. Beside him a body collapsed, limp. It was Max. A shot had gone through his brain. Jim stared down at him, numb with horror.
